A model that fits the data in front of it is not necessarily a model that predicts well. To judge a
survival model as a predictor, or to compare competing models, you need metrics that account for
censoring. Greenwood provides three complementary ones: (1) the concordance index, (measures how
well a model ranks subjects by risk), (2) the Brier score (measures how accurate its probability
predictions are), and (3) the time-dependent AUC (shows how discrimination changes over the
follow-up horizon). This guide page explains all three and shows how to compute them for a fitted
model or for any external risk score.

We start from the `lung` outcomes and a Cox model fit to them. This is the model whose predictions
we will judge.

```{python}
import greenwood as gw

# Load the lung dataset
lung = gw.load_dataset("lung", backend="polars")

# Name the survival response columns, then bind them to the data to display a summary
death = gw.Outcome.surv(time="time", event="status")
death.bind(lung)
```

The response `death` names the follow-up time and event columns, and bound to `lung` it records 165
events among 228 subjects. We fit a Cox model with the same response, then set the model aside:
everything below needs only `death`, the data, and the risk scores and survival probabilities that
`cox` produces. Each metric reads the response columns from the frame passed as `data=`.

```{python}
# Fit a Cox model with age and sex as covariates
cox = gw.CoxPH().fit("Surv(time, status) ~ age + sex", data=lung)
```

## Discrimination: the concordance index

Discrimination is the ability to rank subjects correctly: to give higher risk scores to subjects who
go on to have the event sooner. The concordance index, or C-statistic, measures exactly this. It is
the probability that, for a randomly chosen comparable pair of subjects, the one who failed first
had the higher risk score. A value of 0.5 is no better than a coin flip, and 1.0 is perfect
ordering.

You can compute it for any risk score, which makes it useful for evaluating a model on new data or
for comparing an external score. Here we use the Cox model's linear predictor. Asking for
`type="lp"` returns one number per subject, where a larger value means higher predicted risk.

```{python}
# Rebuild the dataset, response, and Cox fit for this section
lung = gw.load_dataset("lung", backend="polars")

death = gw.Outcome.surv(time="time", event="status")
cox = gw.CoxPH().fit("Surv(time, status) ~ age + sex", data=lung)

# Extract the linear predictor (risk score) for each subject
risk = cox.predict(type="lp")
risk[:8]
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Linear predictors are centered

The linear predictor returned by `predict(type="lp")` is always centered around the mean of the
training covariates. This ensures consistent, numerically stable predictions across all variable
types: continuous, categorical, and mixed. The centering is applied uniformly, so you always get
mathematically sound risk scores, even in edge cases like categorical-only models with all positive
associations.
:::

These are the scores the index will rank against the observed event order. Because higher risk
should correspond to earlier failure, we pass a score where larger means higher risk, such as this
linear predictor or its exponential.

```{python}
# Compute Harrell's concordance index from the risk scores
gw.concordance_index(death, risk=risk, data=lung)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Discrimination is only part of the story

A model can rank subjects well yet produce poorly calibrated probabilities, or vice versa. The
concordance index says nothing about whether predicted probabilities are numerically accurate. That
is what the Brier score adds.
:::

## Censoring-corrected discrimination: the IPCW concordance index

Harrell's C treats censored subjects by simply excluding incomparable pairs. When censoring is light
and roughly uniform, this works well. But when censoring is heavy (more than 30-40% of subjects) or
differs across risk groups, the resulting estimate can be biased because the excluded pairs are not
missing at random.

The IPCW concordance index of Uno et al. (2011) corrects for this by weighting each concordant pair
by the inverse of the censoring probability at the event time. Subjects whose events occur at times
when many others have already been censored receive higher weight, compensating for the information
lost to censoring. The result is a consistent estimator of the true concordance probability.

```{python}
# Rebuild the dataset, response, and Cox fit
lung = gw.load_dataset("lung", backend="polars")

death = gw.Outcome.surv(time="time", event="status")
cox = gw.CoxPH().fit("Surv(time, status) ~ age + sex", data=lung)

# IPCW concordance index corrected for censoring bias
risk = cox.predict(type="lp")
gw.concordance_index_ipcw(death, risk=risk, data=lung)
```

In the `lung` dataset censoring is moderate (~28%), so the IPCW and Harrell values are close. In
datasets with heavier censoring the two can diverge meaningfully. The IPCW version is the safer
default for formal model comparisons.

The `tau` parameter restricts the evaluation to events before a truncation time. This avoids
instability from very small censoring probabilities in the tail, where few subjects remain under
observation. It also focuses discrimination on a clinically relevant horizon.

```{python}
# Restrict evaluation to events before one year
gw.concordance_index_ipcw(death, risk=risk, data=lung, tau=365.0)
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Choosing tau

When the censoring survival function drops close to zero in the tail, the IPCW weights become very
large and the estimate becomes unstable. Setting `tau` to the end of the clinically relevant
follow-up window (for example, one year or five years) avoids this. The default is the largest
observed event time, which works well when censoring remains moderate throughout follow-up.
:::

## Concordance confidence intervals

A point estimate of the concordance is not enough for a formal comparison. You also need a standard
error and a confidence interval. `concordance_index_ci()` computes the IPCW concordance and derives
the standard error from the influence function decomposition, which avoids the cost of
bootstrapping. The confidence interval is constructed on the logit scale (the default), which
respects the [0, 1] bounds and provides better coverage when the estimate is near either extreme.

```{python}
# Rebuild the dataset, response, and Cox fit
lung = gw.load_dataset("lung", backend="polars")

death = gw.Outcome.surv(time="time", event="status")
cox = gw.CoxPH().fit("Surv(time, status) ~ age + sex", data=lung)

# Concordance with standard error and confidence interval
risk = cox.predict(type="lp")
gw.concordance_index_ci(death, risk=risk, data=lung)
```

The result is a `ConcordanceResult` with the point estimate, standard error, and confidence limits.
You can convert it to a one-row DataFrame with `to_frame()`.

```{python}
# Convert the result to a one-row DataFrame
gw.concordance_index_ci(death, risk=risk, data=lung).to_frame()
```

The `transform` parameter controls the scale on which the CI is constructed. The default `"logit"`
is recommended because it keeps the interval inside [0, 1] even when the estimate is close to the
boundary. The `"log"` and `"identity"` options are available for comparison.

```{python}
# Same concordance with an identity-scale confidence interval
gw.concordance_index_ci(death, risk=risk, data=lung, transform="identity")
```

For competing-risks data, pass `cause=` and `tau=` to get the cause-specific concordance with its
CI. This uses the incidence-weighted influence function, which accounts for both standard and
competing-event pairs.

```{python}
import numpy as np

# Load competing-risks data
mgus2 = gw.load_dataset("mgus2", backend="polars")

# The first observed endpoint (PCM at `ptime`, or death at `futime`) is the event
cr = gw.Outcome.first_event(
    endpoints={"pcm": ("ptime", "pstat"), "death": ("futime", "death")},
)

# Fit a Fine-Gray model for PCM and predict CIF at 240 months
fg = gw.FineGray(cause="pcm").fit(cr, covariates=["age", "sex"], data=mgus2)
cif_at_tau = fg.predict_cumulative_incidence(
    mgus2, times=np.array([240.0]), format="pandas"
).drop(columns="time").values.flatten()

# Cause-specific concordance with confidence interval
gw.concordance_index_ci(cr, risk=cif_at_tau, data=mgus2, cause=1, tau=240.0)
```

## Comparing two concordance indices

When two models are fit on the same subjects, their concordance estimates are correlated. A naive
comparison that treats them as independent underestimates uncertainty and inflates the Type I error
rate. The `concordance_index_compare()` function uses the paired influence-function delta method:
it computes the difference in concordance indices and derives the standard error from the joint
influence function, which properly accounts for the shared subjects.

```{python}
# Rebuild the dataset and response
lung = gw.load_dataset("lung", backend="polars")

death = gw.Outcome.surv(time="time", event="status")

# Fit two competing Cox models
cox_full = gw.CoxPH().fit("Surv(time, status) ~ age + sex", data=lung)
cox_age = gw.CoxPH().fit("Surv(time, status) ~ age", data=lung)

# Extract linear predictors from each model
lp_full = cox_full.predict(type="lp")
lp_age = cox_age.predict(type="lp")

# Paired comparison of concordance indices
gw.concordance_index_compare(death, risk_a=lp_full, risk_b=lp_age, data=lung)
```

The result reports the difference (model A minus model B), its standard error, a confidence
interval, a z-statistic, and a two-sided p-value. A small p-value means the two models have
detectably different discrimination on this data. The result also has a `to_frame()` method for
tabular output.

```{python}
# Tabular output of the paired comparison
gw.concordance_index_compare(death, risk_a=lp_full, risk_b=lp_age, data=lung).to_frame()
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## When to use paired comparison vs. cross-validation

`concordance_index_compare()` gives you a formal hypothesis test on a single dataset. Cross-
validation with `cross_validate()` gives you an estimate of out-of-sample performance. They answer
different questions. Use the paired test when you want a p-value for the difference on the observed
data. Use cross-validation when you want to estimate how much better one model will perform on new
subjects.
:::

## The censoring distribution

The IPCW concordance index above works because it knows how likely each subject was to be censored.
That knowledge comes from a `CensoringDistribution`, which estimates the Kaplan-Meier curve of the
censoring process. Greenwood uses it internally for all IPCW metrics, but you can also create one
directly when you need the censoring probabilities or IPC weights for a custom analysis.

```{python}
# Rebuild the dataset and response
lung = gw.load_dataset("lung", backend="polars")
death = gw.Outcome.surv(time="time", event="status")

# Estimate the censoring distribution from the response (it takes a bound `Surv`)
cens = gw.CensoringDistribution(death.bind(lung))
cens
```

The `survival()` method evaluates the censoring survival function G(t), which is the probability of
not being censored by time t, at any set of query times.

```{python}
# Evaluate the censoring survival function G(t) at three times
cens.survival(times=[180, 365, 540])
```

The values decrease over follow-up as more subjects are censored. At 180 days about 97% of subjects
are still under observation, but by 540 days only 57% remain.

The `weights()` method returns the IPC weights that correct for censoring. Each uncensored subject
receives a weight of 1 / G(t-), where G(t-) is the censoring survival just before their event time.
Censored subjects receive weight zero (they are excluded from the reweighted analysis). Subjects
whose events occur when censoring is heavy get larger weights because they represent more unobserved
individuals.

```{python}
# IPC weights: 1/G(t-) for uncensored, 0 for censored
w = cens.weights()
w[:10]
```

You can restrict weights to a time horizon with `tau`. Subjects with events after `tau` receive zero
weight, which avoids instability from very small censoring probabilities in the tail.

```{python}
# Restrict weights to events before one year
cens.weights(tau=365.0)[:10]
```

The full censoring curve is available as a DataFrame via `to_frame()`.

```{python}
# Full censoring curve as a DataFrame
cens.to_frame()
```

## Accuracy: the Brier score

The Brier score is the mean squared error between predicted survival probabilities and actual
outcomes, evaluated at a fixed time. Lower is better. Because outcomes are censored, the score uses
inverse-probability-of-censoring weighting so that censored subjects contribute correctly rather
than being ignored or mishandled.

To compute it you supply predicted survival probabilities for each subject at each evaluation time.
Start by asking the Cox model for survival curves at three fixed times.

```{python}
# Rebuild the dataset, response, and Cox fit
lung = gw.load_dataset("lung", backend="polars")

death = gw.Outcome.surv(time="time", event="status")
cox = gw.CoxPH().fit("Surv(time, status) ~ age + sex", data=lung)

# Predict survival probabilities at three fixed times
times = [180, 365, 540]
surv = cox.predict(lung, type="survival", times=times, format="polars")
surv.shape
```

The returned DataFrame has a leading `time` column and one column per subject, so its shape is 3
rows (the requested times) by 229 columns (228 subjects plus the time column). The Brier score wants
the transpose of this: an array with one row per subject and one column per time. We drop the `time`
column and transpose to get there.

```{python}
# Transpose to (n_subjects, n_times) for the Brier score
probs = surv.drop("time").to_numpy().T
probs.shape
```

With the probabilities in the expected `(n_subjects, n_times)` shape, we can score them.

```{python}
# IPCW Brier score at each evaluation time
gw.brier_score(death, survival_prob=probs, times=times, data=lung)
```

The result is one Brier score per time. As a rule of thumb, a useful model should beat the Brier
score of a model that ignores covariates, and a score approaching 0.25 at a time where about half
the subjects have had the event is close to uninformative.

To summarize accuracy across a range of times in a single number, integrate the Brier score over
time.

```{python}
# Integrated Brier score across the three time horizons
gw.integrated_brier_score(death, survival_prob=probs, times=times, data=lung)
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Evaluate on data the model did not see

Computing these metrics on the same data used to fit the model gives optimistic results. For an
honest assessment, evaluate on a held-out test set or use cross-validation, fitting on one part of
the data and scoring predictions on another.
:::

## Brier score for competing risks

The standard Brier score evaluates predicted survival probabilities. In a competing-risks setting,
the quantity of interest is instead the cumulative incidence function (CIF) for a specific cause.
`brier_score_incidence()` extends the IPCW Brier score to this setting: it compares predicted CIF
probabilities against observed cause-specific outcomes.

The weighting scheme accounts for competing events. Subjects who experienced *any* event (including
a competing cause) before the evaluation time are weighted by the inverse censoring probability at
their event time. Subjects still at risk contribute at the inverse censoring probability at the
evaluation time. Subjects censored before the evaluation time receive zero weight.

To illustrate, we describe a competing-risks response for the `mgus2` dataset, where subjects may
progress to plasma cell malignancy (PCM) or die without progression. `Outcome.first_event()` names
the time and status columns of each endpoint.

```{python}
import numpy as np

# Load competing-risks data
mgus2 = gw.load_dataset("mgus2", backend="polars")

# The first observed endpoint (PCM at `ptime`, or death at `futime`) is the event
cr = gw.Outcome.first_event(
    endpoints={"pcm": ("ptime", "pstat"), "death": ("futime", "death")},
)

# Bind the response to the data to display its summary
cr.bind(mgus2)
```

As a baseline, we use the marginal Aalen-Johansen CIF as a naive model that predicts the same CIF
for every subject.

```{python}
# Fit Aalen-Johansen and extract the marginal PCM incidence curve
aj = gw.AalenJohansen().fit(cr, data=mgus2)
cif_df = aj.to_frame(format="polars")
pcm_cif = cif_df.filter(cif_df["cause"] == "pcm")

# Interpolate the marginal CIF at the evaluation times
times_cr = np.array([60, 120, 240])
marginal = np.array(
    [float(np.interp(t, pcm_cif["time"].to_numpy(), pcm_cif["estimate"].to_numpy()))
     for t in times_cr]
)

# Tile the marginal CIF across all subjects and compute the Brier score
probs_cr = np.tile(marginal, (mgus2.height, 1))
gw.brier_score_incidence(cr, incidence_prob=probs_cr, times=times_cr, data=mgus2, cause=1)
```

The `cause=` argument selects which event code to evaluate. Here `cause=1` corresponds to
progression (the first endpoint listed in `endpoints=`). To evaluate death predictions instead,
pass `cause=2`.

As with the survival Brier score, you can summarize accuracy over a range of times in a single
number with the integrated version.

```{python}
# Evaluate the integrated Brier score on a finer grid
times_fine = np.linspace(30, 360, 12)
marginal_fine = np.array(
    [float(np.interp(t, pcm_cif["time"].to_numpy(), pcm_cif["estimate"].to_numpy()))
     for t in times_fine]
)
probs_fine = np.tile(marginal_fine, (mgus2.height, 1))
gw.integrated_brier_score_incidence(
    cr, incidence_prob=probs_fine, times=times_fine, data=mgus2, cause=1
)
```

A model that uses covariates to produce subject-specific CIF predictions should yield a lower
integrated Brier score than this marginal baseline.

## Concordance for competing risks

The standard concordance index evaluates discrimination for a single event type. In a
competing-risks setting, `concordance_index_incidence()` extends the IPCW concordance to
cause-specific cumulative incidence predictions (Wolbers et al., 2014). It compares two types of
pairs: standard pairs (a subject who experienced the cause of interest vs. a subject still at risk)
and competing-event pairs (a subject who experienced the cause vs. one who experienced a competing
event). Each pair type receives its own IPCW weight.

Using the same `mgus2` competing-risks data from above, we evaluate the concordance of the marginal
Aalen-Johansen CIF at 240 months. Because the marginal model predicts the same value for every
subject, its concordance is 0.5 (no discrimination).

```{python}
# Marginal CIF at tau=240 months: same prediction for everyone
tau = 240.0
marginal_at_tau = float(
    np.interp(tau, pcm_cif["time"].to_numpy(), pcm_cif["estimate"].to_numpy())
)
pred_flat = np.full(mgus2.height, marginal_at_tau)

# Concordance for the flat prediction (expected to be 0.5)
gw.concordance_index_incidence(cr, incidence_prob=pred_flat, data=mgus2, cause=1, tau=tau)
```

A model that produces subject-specific CIF predictions should achieve a concordance above 0.5.

## Calibration for competing risks

Beyond discrimination, a model's predicted CIF values should match the observed incidence on
average. `calibration_incidence()` checks marginal calibration by comparing the mean predicted CIF
at each time against the nonparametric Aalen-Johansen reference. The result is the absolute
calibration error at each time point.

```{python}
# Calibration check: mean predicted CIF vs. AJ reference
cal_err = gw.calibration_incidence(
    cr, incidence_prob=probs_cr, times=times_cr, data=mgus2, cause=1
)
cal_err
```

Because the marginal model *is* the AJ reference, its calibration error is essentially zero. A
subject-specific model will typically show nonzero errors, especially in the tails.

## Accuracy in time for competing risks

When the model predicts CIFs for all competing causes, `accuracy_in_time()` evaluates whether the
model correctly identifies the most likely outcome at each time horizon. At time $\zeta$, each
subject's predicted outcome is the argmax of the predicted CIFs plus the implied survival
probability. The metric reports the proportion of uncensored subjects whose predicted class matches
the observed outcome.

```{python}
# Interpolate both CIFs at the evaluation times
death_cif = cif_df.filter(cif_df["cause"] == "death")
pcm_vals = np.array(
    [float(np.interp(t, pcm_cif["time"].to_numpy(), pcm_cif["estimate"].to_numpy()))
     for t in times_cr]
)
death_vals = np.array(
    [float(np.interp(t, death_cif["time"].to_numpy(), death_cif["estimate"].to_numpy()))
     for t in times_cr]
)
# Stack into (n_subjects, n_causes, n_times) and compute accuracy
probs_3d = np.stack(
    [np.tile(pcm_vals, (mgus2.height, 1)), np.tile(death_vals, (mgus2.height, 1))], axis=1
)

gw.accuracy_in_time(cr, incidence_probs=probs_3d, times=times_cr, data=mgus2)
```

Early times tend to show high accuracy because most subjects have survived and the model predicts
survival. The metric becomes most informative at later times, when discriminating between competing
events matters.

## Bundled competing-risks scoring

When evaluating a competing-risks model you typically want concordance, per-time Brier scores, and
the integrated Brier score all at once. `score_cr()` computes them in a single call and returns a
tidy summary table. The concordance row includes a confidence interval from the influence function.
The Brier rows report point estimates only.

```{python}
import numpy as np

# Load data and build competing-risks response
mgus2 = gw.load_dataset("mgus2", backend="polars")

# The first observed endpoint (PCM at `ptime`, or death at `futime`) is the event
cr = gw.Outcome.first_event(
    endpoints={"pcm": ("ptime", "pstat"), "death": ("futime", "death")},
)

# Fit Fine-Gray for PCM and predict CIF at three horizons
fg = gw.FineGray(cause="pcm").fit(cr, covariates=["age", "sex"], data=mgus2)

eval_times = np.array([120, 240, 360])
cif_pred = fg.predict_cumulative_incidence(
    mgus2, times=eval_times, format="pandas"
).drop(columns="time").values.T

# Bundle concordance, Brier, and integrated Brier into one summary
gw.score_cr(cr, incidence_prob=cif_pred, data=mgus2, cause=1, times=eval_times)
```

The `incidence_prob` argument expects a matrix with shape `(n_subjects, n_times)`, where each column
holds the predicted CIF at the corresponding evaluation time. The `cause` argument selects the event
code and the `tau` parameter (defaulting to the last evaluation time) truncates the concordance
calculation.

This is the competing-risks counterpart of running `concordance_index_ci()`,
`brier_score_incidence()`, and `integrated_brier_score_incidence()` separately. When you only need
one of those metrics, calling them individually is fine. The `score_cr()` function saves repetitive
setup when you want the full picture.

## Time-dependent discrimination: AUC over time

The concordance index summarises discrimination with a single number across all event times. But a
marker's ability to separate early failures from survivors often changes over follow-up: a biomarker
may identify six-month events well but lose its signal at five years. `time_dependent_auc()` gives
you a per-horizon view by computing the area under the ROC curve separately at each requested time.

At each time $t$, the estimator compares *cases* (subjects who had an event by $t$) against
*controls* (subjects still at risk after $t$), and measures how well the marker separates the two
groups. Inverse-probability-of-censoring weights correct for the fact that not all subjects are
observed to the end of follow-up. The marker must be on a scale where larger means higher risk, so,
the Cox linear predictor is a natural choice.

```{python}
# Time-dependent AUC at three horizons using the Cox linear predictor
lp = cox.predict(type="lp")
gw.time_dependent_auc(death, marker=lp, times=[180, 365, 540], data=lung)
```

Each value is the AUC at one horizon. Values above 0.5 mean the marker separates early failures from
survivors better than chance at that time. Values close to 0.5 signal that the marker has lost
predictive power at that horizon.

To reduce these to a single number for model comparison, `integrated_auc()` computes the
time-averaged AUC using the trapezoidal rule over the supplied time range.

```{python}
# Time-averaged AUC across the three horizons
gw.integrated_auc(death, marker=lp, times=[180, 365, 540], data=lung)
```

The integrated AUC plays the same role as the integrated Brier score: it collapses time-specific
discrimination into one comparison-friendly number. Higher is better, and 0.5 is the random
baseline.

## Cross-validation

Rather than splitting the data by hand, `cross_validate()` runs k-fold cross-validation for you: it
fits a fresh copy of the model on each set of training folds and scores its predictions on the
held-out fold. Pass an unfitted model and a formula naming the response and the covariates.

```{python}
# Rebuild the dataset
lung = gw.load_dataset("lung", backend="polars")

# Five-fold cross-validated concordance
gw.cross_validate(
    gw.CoxPH(), "Surv(time, status) ~ age + sex", data=lung, k=5, metric="concordance", seed=23
)
```

The result reports the score on each fold plus their mean and standard deviation. The
cross-validated concordance is usually a little lower than the value computed on the training data,
which is exactly the optimism we are trying to remove. Set `metric="brier"` with a list of `times`
to cross-validate the integrated Brier score instead. The same call works for `AFT` and
`RoystonParmar` models.

```{python}
# Cross-validated integrated Brier score at three time points
gw.cross_validate(
    gw.CoxPH(), "Surv(time, status) ~ age + sex", data=lung, k=5,
    metric="brier", times=[180, 365, 540], seed=23
)
```

### Multi-metric mode

When you want concordance, Brier, and AUC together, pass `metrics=` (plural) instead of `metric=`.
The model is fit once per fold and scored on every requested metric, so you get consistent fold
assignments and avoid redundant refitting.

```{python}
# Multi-metric cross-validation: concordance, Brier, and AUC in one pass
result_multi = gw.cross_validate(
    gw.CoxPH(), "Surv(time, status) ~ age + sex", data=lung, k=5,
    metrics=["concordance", "brier", "auc"],
    times=[180, 365, 540], seed=23
)
result_multi
```

The return value is a keyed dictionary. Each metric has its own `scores`, `mean`, and `std`:

```{python}
# Mean cross-validated concordance
result_multi["results"]["concordance"]["mean"]
```

```{python}
# Mean cross-validated integrated Brier score
result_multi["results"]["brier"]["mean"]
```

### Stratified folds for imbalanced data

By default, `cross_validate()` uses stratified k-fold splitting. Rather than randomly assigning
subjects to folds, it groups subjects by event status first, then draws from each group
proportionally. This ensures that each fold contains roughly the same fraction of events as the
overall dataset.

This matters whenever events are rare. In a dataset where only 10% of subjects have the event, pure
random splitting could easily put all events in one fold and none in another, leaving training sets
without enough events to fit the model at all. Stratification prevents that. You can opt out with
`stratified=False`, but there is rarely a good reason to.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Watch the event count

`cross_validate()` warns when the total number of events is less than twice the number of folds. At
that point, some test folds will contain only one event, making per-fold scores unreliable:

```
UserWarning: Only 6 events found for 5-fold cross-validation
(fewer than 2 × k = 10). Some folds may contain too few events
for reliable evaluation. Consider reducing k or collecting more
data with observed events.
```

If you see this warning, either reduce `k=` to match the event count (e.g., `k=3` with 6 events) or
treat the cross-validated scores with caution.
:::

### Comparing models

Cross-validation is most useful as a comparison tool. Fit the same folds on two competing models,
keeping the same `seed`, and compare their mean scores directly. The model with higher mean
concordance (or lower mean Brier score) generalizes better to unseen subjects.

```{python}
# Rebuild the dataset
lung = gw.load_dataset("lung", backend="polars")

# Define two models: simple and full
formula_simple = "Surv(time, status) ~ age + sex"
formula_full = "Surv(time, status) ~ age + sex + ph.ecog"

# Cross-validate both models with the same seed for matched folds
simple_cv = gw.cross_validate(gw.CoxPH(), formula_simple, data=lung, seed=1)
full_cv = gw.cross_validate(gw.CoxPH(), formula_full, data=lung, seed=1)

# Compare mean concordance and fold-to-fold variability
print(f"Simple model  C-index: {simple_cv['mean']:.3f} ± {simple_cv['std']:.3f}")
print(f"Full model    C-index: {full_cv['mean']:.3f} ± {full_cv['std']:.3f}")
```

The standard deviation across folds gives a rough sense of how stable the estimate is. Large
fold-to-fold variation (relative to the difference between models) means the data do not contain
enough information to reliably distinguish the two models on this metric alone.

## Calibration

Discrimination and the Brier score both summarize a model in a single number. Calibration asks a
more detailed question: at a chosen time, do the predicted survival probabilities match what
actually happens? The `calibration()` function groups subjects into bins by their predicted survival
at a horizon, then compares the mean prediction in each bin against the observed survival, a
Kaplan-Meier estimate for that bin.

```{python}
# Rebuild the dataset, response, and Cox fit
lung = gw.load_dataset("lung", backend="polars")

death = gw.Outcome.surv(time="time", event="status")
cox = gw.CoxPH().fit("Surv(time, status) ~ age + sex", data=lung)

# Predict one-year survival for each subject
surv_at_year = cox.predict(
    lung, type="survival", times=[365.0], format="polars"
)

# Extract predictions as a flat array and compute calibration by quintile
predicted = surv_at_year.slice(0, 1).drop("time").to_numpy().flatten()

gw.calibration(death, predicted=predicted, time=365.0, data=lung, n_bins=5, format="polars")
```

Each row is a bin, from the lowest predicted survival to the highest. A well-calibrated model has
`observed` close to `predicted` in every bin, with the observed values inside their confidence
limits. Systematic gaps, for example predictions consistently higher than observed, signal
miscalibration even when discrimination is good.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Assess calibration out of sample too

Like the other metrics, calibration is optimistic on the training data. For a fair picture, compute
it on held-out predictions, for instance the test-fold predictions from a cross-validation split.
:::
